method: OPEN AND QUOTED from International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group' (2020). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at PMC JATS XML <license> element for PMC7469861 (NCBI efetch; Europe PMC returned 503)). Source text: NCBI efetch JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 503 on 2026-09-23); xref ref-type 'ref' normalised to 'bibr' so pmc_text.py strips citation markers as it does for Europe PMC XML.

claims.claim: **Typical picture:** epilepsy starting in infancy, slowing head growth, delayed development and complex movement disorders.
claims.source_text: Patients classically present with infantile‐onset epilepsy, deceleration of head growth, impaired neurological growth and development, and complex movement disorders.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Think of Glut1DS with:** an unexplained movement disorder (spasticity, dystonia, ataxia); drug-resistant epilepsy that is fully controlled by a ketogenic diet; unexplained paroxysmal events at any age; absence epilepsy starting before age 4; or myoclonic-atonic (Doose) epilepsy.
claims.source_text: Clinical features consistent with Glut1DS include the following Any unexplained movement disorder with spasticity, dystonia, and ataxia, Complete seizure control by KDT in children with drug‐resistant epilepsy, Unexplained paroxysmal events at any age, Early‐onset absence epilepsy (under 4 years of age), and Myoclonic‐atonic epilepsy (Doose syndrome).
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Paroxysmal eye-head movements in infancy** were judged specific for Glut1DS by nearly all expert centres (12 of 13).
claims.source_text: Paroxysmal eye‐head movements in infancy were felt to be specific for Glut1DS (12 of 13 centers; 92%)
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Movement problems are typically worse before meals and better after eating,** and are often brought on by fasting or exercise.
claims.source_text: The movements can be persistent or paroxysmal, classically present preprandially, and are mitigated by meals. … These movement abnormalities are frequent and often precipitated by fasting and exercise.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The picture changes with age:** seizures dominate in infants and young children, then tend to fade; movement disorders become the main problem in adolescents and adults.
claims.source_text: Epilepsy tends to be the major clinical problem in infants and young children with Glut1DS, whereas seizures tend to decline or disappear in later childhood, adolescence, and adulthood.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The hallmark is low CSF glucose with normal blood glucose (hypoglycorrhachia)**, with CSF lactate low-normal or low, which separates it from mitochondrial disease. Exclude other causes first: hypoglycaemia, meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, or a VP shunt.
claims.source_text: Low CSF glucose values in the setting of normoglycemia, termed hypoglycorrhachia, represent the metabolic hallmark of Glut1DS. … Other causes of hypoglycorrhachia such as hypoglycemia, meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or ventriculoperitoneal shunt systems need to be excluded. … In Glut1DS, CSF lactate levels are always low‐normal or abnormally low, separating this condition from other diseases causing impaired brain energy metabolism, most notably mitochondrial diseases.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do the lumbar puncture after a four- to six-hour fast,** and measure blood glucose immediately beforehand to avoid a stress-related rise.
claims.source_text: The lumbar puncture should be performed in a postabsorptive state following a four‐ to six‐hour fast. Blood glucose measurements should be determined immediately prior to performing the lumbar puncture to avoid stress‐related hyperglycemia.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CSF glucose cut-off:** classically below 2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL); milder cases can sit at 2.2 to 2.9 mmol/L, but are never normal.
claims.source_text: Hypoglycorrhachia in typical Glut1DS was originally defined as a cutoff value of 2.2 mmol/L (40 mg/dL). … It is now clear that milder phenotypes may have CSF values of 2.2 to 2.9 mmol/L (41‐52 mg/dL), but never normal.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **SLC2A1 testing:** sequencing finds a variant in 81%–89%, and deletion/duplication analysis a further 11%–14%. A negative result does not exclude Glut1DS.
claims.source_text: Sequence analysis identifies heterozygous de pathogenic variants (or rarely, biallelic pathogenic variants) in SLC2A1 in 81%‐89% of patients. Another 11%‐14% of patients are confirmed by deletion/duplication analysis. However, the absence of SLC2A1 pathogenic variants does not always exclude Glut1DS.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A definite diagnosis needs all three:** characteristic clinical features, hypoglycorrhachia and a pathogenic SLC2A1 variant. With characteristic features, most experts accept two of the three.
claims.source_text: All authors agreed that the definite diagnosis of Glut1DS requires the presence of characteristic clinical features, hypoglycorrhachia, and a pathogenic variant in SLC2A1 (13/13, 100%). Controversies arose when some of these diagnostic criteria were negative or of unclear significance (survey question 1). In the presence of characteristic clinical features, most experts felt that two of three criteria were sufficient for the diagnosis.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Ketogenic diet therapy (KDT) is the treatment of choice; start it as early as possible.** All 13 centres agreed.
claims.source_text: Ketogenic diet therapies remain the treatment of choice for Glut1DS and should be started as early as possible (13/13, 100%, survey questions 4,5,8).
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Under two years, use a classical 3:1 ketogenic diet.**
claims.source_text: In children under age two years, a classical 3:1 KDT is the treatment of choice.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The modified Atkins diet is a good alternative** for adolescents, adults and patients who cannot keep to the classical diet.
claims.source_text: Most centers also believe that for adolescents, adults, and noncompliant patients, the MAD provides a good alternative to the classical KDT (12/13, 92%).
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not use the low glycaemic index treatment:** it produces very little ketosis and has no evidence of benefit in Glut1DS.
claims.source_text: The low glycemic index treatment (LGIT) provides very low ketones, has no evidence of benefit for Glut1DS, and is not recommended.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor ketosis with blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (target 2–5 mmol/L)**, not urine ketones, which are only qualitative.
claims.source_text: All patients with Glut1DS should monitor their ketosis by determination of beta‐hydroxybutyrate in capillary or venous blood. Urine ketones are a qualitative measure of acetoacetate and as such are not as adequate to quantitatively monitor ketonemia in Glut1DS patients. … essential blood ketone measurements targeting 2‐5 mmol/L for blood beta‐hydroxybutyrate
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not stop the diet after two years** as in other epilepsies: benefit is thought to continue into adulthood, so continue it for as long as it is tolerated.
claims.source_text: Although most children with epilepsy on KDT can be transitioned off this treatment after two years, this plan is not appropriate for a child with Glut1DS. The benefits of KDT have no clear "end‐date" and are thought to extend into adulthood. … All centers recommend continuing the KDT for as long as tolerated by the patient.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Check carnitine levels,** because patients on the diet can become carnitine-deficient over time.
claims.source_text: Carnitine levels need to be monitored as patients may become secondarily carnitine‐deficient over time.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No antiseizure drug can be recommended:** none treats the underlying defect, and some may interact harmfully with the diet.
claims.source_text: Treating Glut1DS with antiseizure medications does not address the underlying metabolic defect. … Currently, there is no basis to recommend any antiseizure drug in the management of Glut1DS, and there are concerns regarding potential harmful interactions with KDT
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Drugs to be wary of:** carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, topiramate, sulthiame) can worsen acidosis; topiramate, acetazolamide and zonisamide raise kidney-stone risk on the diet; barbiturates, diazepam, valproate and others inhibit Glut1 in the laboratory.
claims.source_text: For example, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide, topiramate, and sulthiame may aggravate acidosis. Topiramate, acetazolamide, and zonisamide may increase the risk of urolithiasis, especially in combination with KDT. … Barbiturates, diazepam, sodium valproate, chloralhydrate, methylxanthine, and ethanol are nonspecific inhibitors of Glut1 function in vitro.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Triheptanoin is not an evidence-based option:** its phase 3 trial in Glut1DS missed its primary and secondary endpoints.
claims.source_text: a phase 3 study of triheptanoin (UX007) for the treatment of Glut1DS (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01993186) failed to meet its primary and secondary endpoints.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adults:** consider a pregnancy test before starting a ketogenic diet in women of childbearing age (teratogenic risk unknown). The modified Atkins diet is a reasonable choice for poorly controlled seizures or paroxysmal movement disorders.
claims.source_text: for women of childbearing age, a pregnancy test should be considered prior to a KDT given that the risks of teratogenicity are unknown. … In general, the modified Atkins diet (MAD) is considered a reasonable alternative for adolescents and adults, when treating poorly controlled seizures and paroxysmal movement disorders.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor long-term diet effects regularly:** kidney stones, growth, and cardiovascular risk (blood pressure, fasting lipids, and transcranial Doppler from age 10).
claims.source_text: There was general agreement that patients should be monitored regularly for long‐term side effects of KDT such as kidney stones, growth retardation, and cardiovascular disease (blood pressure, fasting lipid profiles, transcranial Doppler ultrasound from age 10 years).
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Plan the transition to adult care** for both diet therapy and medical follow-up.
claims.source_text: With patients approaching adulthood, it is critical to develop a transitional plan for diet therapy and for medical care to transition from a pediatric to an adult subspecialist.
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not stop the ketogenic diet to join a trial of a new treatment:** the group strongly rejected this.
claims.source_text: Discontinuing KDT, the current standard of care for Glut1DS, in favor of clinical trials that are designed to investigate novel treatment considerations was rejected strongly by the group (12/13, 92%).
claims.locator: International Glut1DS Study Group (Klepper J et al.), Epilepsia Open, 'Glut1 Deficiency Syndrome (Glut1DS): State of the art in 2020 and recommendations of the international Glut1DS study group', 2020, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7469861/, retrieved 2026-09-23
